```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, dpi = 96)
```

visualbrief covers the whole path from a campaign export to a report you can
send: standardise the data, summarise it, compare content across audiences
with honest uncertainty, follow it over time, and present it with an
accessible visual identity.

```{r}
library(visualbrief)
```

## 1. Standardise the data

Every platform names its columns differently. `vb_campaign()` maps them to
eleven standard fields; only `impressions` is required.

```{r}
raw <- data.frame(
  Day = c("2026-03-02", "2026-03-02", "2026-03-03", "2026-03-03"),
  `Ad name` = c("Video", "Carousel", "Video", "Carousel"),
  Impressions = c(1200, 950, 1300, 1010),
  `Link clicks` = c(36, 19, 41, 22),
  check.names = FALSE
)
vb_campaign(raw, date = "Day", content = "Ad name",
            impressions = "Impressions", clicks = "Link clicks")
```

`vb_read_csv()` does the same from a file, including the semicolon-separated
files with decimal commas that spreadsheets produce in many European
locales.

The rest of this guide uses `campaign_demo`, a **synthetic** campaign with
known effects: four pieces of content, three audiences, three channels and
twelve weeks.

```{r}
campaign_demo
```

## 2. Summarise

```{r}
s <- vb_summarise(campaign_demo, by = "channel")
s[, c("channel", "impressions", "clicks", "ctr", "ctr_low", "ctr_high", "cpa")]
```

Rates come with Wilson 95% intervals, which behave well for the small
proportions typical of click-through and conversion. Summed reach is an upper
bound: the same person may be reached on several days or channels.

## 3. Which content works with each audience?

```{r, fig.height = 6.5}
vb_plot_rates(campaign_demo, metric = "ctr", by = "content", within = "audience")
```

`vb_compare()` puts numbers on what the chart shows. Within each audience,
every piece is compared with the most delivered one, with the difference, its
interval (Newcombe's hybrid score method) and a test adjusted for the number
of comparisons (Holm).

```{r}
cmp <- vb_compare(campaign_demo, metric = "ctr", by = "content", within = "audience")
cmp[cmp$audience == "Researchers",
    c("content", "rate", "diff", "diff_low", "diff_high", "p_adjusted", "small_sample")]
```

The analysis recovers the effects built into the data: the infographic works
best with researchers, the testimonial with professionals and the video with
students.

**What this does and does not show.** Unless the campaign was a randomised
test, these are descriptions of what happened, not proof that one piece
causes better results: platforms decide who sees what, timing changes, and
audiences overlap. visualbrief reports intervals and flags small samples so
that readers do not over-interpret noise.

## 4. Over time

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
vb_plot_trend(campaign_demo, metric = "ctr", by = "channel")
```

The decline in every channel is the creative fatigue simulated in the data.

## 5. An accessible visual identity

```{r}
brand <- vb_brand("Acme research", primary = "#1F4E5F",
                  palette = c("#1F4E5F", "#B35900", "#007A5E", "#E69F00"))
vb_check_contrast(brand)
```

The light orange fails the 3:1 contrast that WCAG 2.2 requires for chart
elements: replace it before using the palette. If your organisation keeps a
`_brand.yml` file for Quarto or Shiny, `vb_brand_yml()` reads it, so one
identity serves charts, reports and websites.

## 6. The report

```{r, eval = FALSE}
vb_report(campaign_demo, "campaign-report.html",
          title = "Spring awareness campaign", brand = vb_brand("Acme research"),
          currency = "EUR")
```

The result is a single HTML file, with no external resources, that you can
email or archive. It contains the headline figures, results by channel, the
comparison with intervals, the trend, the colour accessibility check and a
plain-language note on method. For a report with your own text and sections,
`vb_quarto_template()` copies an editable Quarto document.
